articles.title: Casio’s adjustable G-Shock ring watch launches in the US next week.
articles.summary:
If you skipped Casio’s original ring watch because it relied on spacers to improve its fit, the new DWN-5600 can be resized from 48mm to 82mm using an adjustable strap like a full size G-Shock. It launched in Japan last month, but will be available in the US starting on December 3rd for $110.00.

articles.title: Dave Bautista Gains 20 Lbs. of Muscle in 2 Months for “God of War”
articles.summary: The Marvel alum shared that he now weighs 250 lbs. in an update on his fitness preparation for the hotly anticipated video game adaptation
articles.body:
Dave Bautista gained 20 lbs. of muscle in two months for Amazon Prime's God of War series

Bautista plays the mythological warrior Kratos after Ryan Hurst left the role because of an injury

The PlayStation adaptation is expected to premiere in 2027

Dave Bautista revealed that he's gained 20 lbs. of muscle in two months to prepare for his role as the mythological warrior Kratos in the upcoming action series God of War .

"Gained 20 lbs. for GOW ," the Guardians of the Galaxy alum, 57, shared in an update to his Instagram stories on Nov. 2, where he flexed his hard-earned muscles in a black God of War T-shirt. Bautista added a GIF that said "250," apparently alluding to his current weight.

The post comes two months after he shared a shirtless progress update on Sept. 2, just three weeks into weight training.

"2 more months to get to where I need to be. Like ridin a bike! LFG!💪🏽," Bautista, who famously played the buff, shirtless superhero Drax in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, wrote on the post.

Bautista landed the role of Kratos in Amazon Prime's hotly anticipated God of War series in August after Ryan Hurst , who had originally been cast in the role, had to bow out due to an injury. The series is set to premiere in 2027, and is based on a beloved PlayStation franchise .

Take PEOPLE with you! Subscribe to PEOPLE magazine to get the latest details on celebrity news, exclusive royal updates, how-it-happened true crime stories and more — right to your mailbox.

The WWE alum is no stranger to dramatic weight transformations to suit a role: Bautista previously shared that, after bulking up for 2023's Knock at the Cabin , he began doing jiu-jitsu and eating a balanced diet to shed 75 lbs. by late 2024.

"I started slimming down because I ... was uncomfortably big. Now looking back at it, I probably overdid it," he said on the Insight with Chris Van Vliet podcast in September 2024, adding that he put on extra pounds by eating pancakes and French fries. "At the time, I was just thinking, 'I gotta get big, I gotta get big.' "

images.caption: Dave Bautista gained 20 bs. of muscle for 'God of War' Credit: Dave Bautista/Instagram
Dave Bautista shared his progress 3 months into his weight-training program Credit: Dave Bautista/Instagram

articles.title: Honda City 2027 muda pouco e não baixa preços para enfrentar os chineses; veja o teste | G1
articles.standfirst: Com preços iguais aos da linha anterior, marca aposta nos clientes fiéis e na reputação do pós-venda. Modelo ganhou novo visual, mais equipamentos e garantia de seis anos, mas manteve o motor aspirado e câmbio CVT.
articles.summary: Com preços iguais aos da linha anterior, marca aposta nos clientes fiéis e na reputação do pós-venda. Modelo ganhou novo visual, mais equipamentos e garantia de seis anos, mas manteve o motor aspirado e câmbio CVT.
articles.body:
Honda City 2027. — Foto: Divulgação / Honda

A Honda apresentou a linha 2027 do City sem reduzir os preços para enfrentar a concorrência dos carros chineses. As versões custam entre R$ 117 mil e R$ 156 mil.

A fabricante aposta na fidelidade de seus clientes e no pós-venda para manter as vendas do modelo, que ganhou mudanças no visual, novos equipamentos e uma versão inédita.

Além da nova versão RS, o City hatch e o sedã receberam alterações nos para-choques, faróis e acabamento. As configurações mais caras também passaram a oferecer uma central multimídia de 10 polegadas.

O motor 1.5 aspirado de 126 cv e o câmbio automático CVT continuam os mesmos. E o g1 testou o novo Honda City para entender se apenas quem é fã da marca japonesa vai ficar feliz com a novidade.

Toda a família City passou por uma atualização visual, concentrada principalmente na dianteira. A Honda redesenhou os para-choques e passou a oferecer faróis Full LED de série em todas as configurações.

Nas versões Touring e RS, uma barra iluminada em LED conecta visualmente os faróis dianteiros e funciona como luz de posição.

Outra mudança aparece ao redor do logotipo da Honda. A região recebeu uma moldura pintada na cor da carroceria, que cria a impressão de que o capô ficou mais comprido.

A grade superior agora apresenta acabamento em formato de colmeia e uma pequena inclinação. O desenho da parte inferior do para-choque continua diferente entre as duas carrocerias.

No sedã, a entrada de ar inferior tem formato de trapézio invertido, com barras horizontais. Já o hatch utiliza uma grade em colmeia, acompanhada por uma seção pintada na cor do veículo.

A traseira também foi modificada. O sedã ganhou um para-choque com desenho trapezoidal e refletores verticais nas extremidades.

No hatch, os recortes do para-choque traseiro ficaram mais afilados.

As rodas de liga leve de 16 polegadas receberam novos acabamentos, com tonalidades de cinza ou preto conforme a versão.

As mudanças mais significativas do Honda City 2027, portanto, estão no design. Ao vivo, o conjunto é harmonioso, mesmo com a adoção de elementos visuais inspirados no Prelude.

Adaptar características de um carro para outro mais barato e com proporções diferentes nem sempre funciona, mas, neste caso, a Honda conseguiu um resultado equilibrado.

O curioso é que, ao tentar atualizar o City sem modificar profundamente o projeto, a fabricante acaba revisitando soluções já utilizadas.

Os refletores dos para-choques, por exemplo, começaram com formato vertical, passaram a ser horizontais no facelift e agora voltaram à posição vertical.

É uma demonstração de como a linguagem visual adotada pela Honda oferece poucas possibilidades de mudanças mais profundas sem alterar a identidade do modelo.

A Honda não alterou a mecânica do City 2027 . Tanto o hatch quanto o sedã continuam equipados com motor 1.5 flex aspirado de quatro cilindros, com bloco e cabeçote de alumínio e injeção direta de combustível.

São 126 cv de potência com etanol ou gasolina. O torque máximo chega a 15,8 kgfm com etanol e 15,5 kgfm com gasolina.

O câmbio também permanece o automático CVT, que simula trocas de marcha.

A transmissão tem ainda uma função que aumenta automaticamente o freio-motor durante descidas, quando o sistema identifica o acionamento do pedal de freio.

O consumo informado para cada carroceria é o seguinte:

Etanol : Cidade 9,1 km/l; Estrada 10,8 km/l

Gasolina : Cidade 12,9 km/l; Estrada 15,3 km/l

Etanol : Cidade 9,1 km/l; Estrada 10,7 km/l

Gasolina : Cidade 13,2 km/l; Estrada 15,1 km/l

Na mecânica, o motor 1.5 aspirado continua sendo um dos pontos fortes do City, principalmente pela previsibilidade de manutenção e pelo comportamento conhecido dos proprietários.

Se o objetivo da Honda é preservar as características valorizadas pelos clientes, a decisão faz sentido. Tanto o sedã quanto o hatch continuam sendo produtos bem resolvidos, com um conjunto mecânico que não apresenta surpresas.

O g1 dirigiu o City em rodovias e trechos de estradas sinuosas. Como não houve mudanças mecânicas, o comportamento permaneceu dentro do esperado.

O desempenho não está entre os principais atributos do modelo, mas isso não significa que o motor 1.5 aspirado seja muito inferior aos modelos 1.0 turbo disponíveis no mercado.

O consumo também chamou a atenção. Em determinados momentos da viagem, mantendo velocidade de cruzeiro entre 100 km/h e 110 km/h, o computador de bordo indicou consumo de gasolina de 21 km/l.

Isso mostra que motoristas dispostos a dirigir de maneira mais tranquila conseguem aproveitar a eficiência do conjunto mecânico.

Detalhes da cabine da linha 2027 do Honda City.

Na cabine, uma das principais novidades é a central multimídia com tela sensível ao toque de 10 polegadas, disponível nas versões Touring e RS.

O equipamento permite controlar o volume e trocar de música por meio de gestos com vários dedos na tela.

A conexão com Android Auto e Apple CarPlay funciona sem a necessidade de cabos.

Essa nova central multimídia ajuda a entender a filosofia da Honda em relação aos seus clientes mais tradicionais. Em vez de apostar em uma interface repleta de cores e efeitos visuais, a fabricante optou por uma apresentação mais discreta, com fundo preto e comandos simplificados.

Embora não tenha botões físicos, a central permite realizar algumas operações deslizando os dedos pela tela . É uma solução interessante do ponto de vista da ergonomia, pois busca facilitar o uso dos comandos sem exigir que o motorista desvie constantemente o olhar da estrada.

A escolha, porém, também representa uma aposta comercial. Ao priorizar a objetividade, a Honda pode agradar aos compradores acostumados com seus produtos, mas deixar de conquistar consumidores que valorizam telas maiores e interfaces mais chamativas.

Para esse público, uma central de apenas 10 polegadas, com fundo preto e poucos efeitos gráficos, pode transmitir a impressão de ser inferior a sistemas mais coloridos, mesmo que isso não seja a verdade.

A segurança também recebeu atualizações. Todas as versões do City 2027 passaram a contar com seis airbags. Já o pacote de assistência à condução Honda Sensing agora é de série nas configurações EX, EXL, Touring e RS.

Entre os recursos estão a frenagem automática para reduzir o risco de colisões e o assistente que ajuda a manter o carro dentro da faixa de circulação.

O controle de cruzeiro adaptativo também foi atualizado. Agora, consegue acompanhar o veículo à frente em velocidades baixas e realizar uma parada completa.

A partir da configuração EXL, o City passa a oferecer o sistema myHonda Connect, que permite utilizar um aplicativo de celular para consultar a localização do carro e comandar funções à distância, como o ar-condicionado.

Outra mudança é a garantia de fábrica, ampliada para seis anos em toda a linha, sem limite de quilometragem.

Honda City 2027 tem parachoques dianteiros exclusivos para cada carroceria — Foto: Divulgação / Honda

O g1 questionou executivos da Honda sobre a decisão de manter os preços do City em um momento de maior concorrência dos fabricantes chineses.

Ariel Mógor, gerente de marketing da Honda, afirmou que a empresa não pretende disputar clientes por meio de descontos agressivos.

“A Honda tem altos índices de satisfação no pós-venda e temos um retorno dos clientes que já são Honda”, explicou.

Segundo o executivo, a fabricante considera que as atualizações da linha 2027, acompanhadas de reajustes relativamente pequenos, são suficientes para atender ao público do City.

A Honda também aposta na rede de concessionárias, que possui uma estratégia de valorização dos carros seminovos da marca nas negociações por veículos zero-quilômetro.

Entre janeiro e agosto de 2026, a fabricante emplacou 18.909 unidades da família City no Brasil. As vendas ganharam ritmo a partir de julho e alcançaram os melhores resultados do ano nos meses seguintes.

A estratégia, porém, ocorre em um momento de mudanças nos preços dos carros novos e usados.

O g1 mostrou que o mercado passou por ajustes importantes em 2026 , impulsionados principalmente pela chegada de novos modelos chineses na faixa de R$ 100 mil a R$ 200 mil, segmento em que o City também está presente.

Veja alguns exemplos de carros com projetos da China na faixa de R$ 125 mil a R$ 150 mil com boa lista de equipamentos:

BYD Dolphin GS : R$ 150 mil (promoção de R$ 139.990)

Chevrolet Spark EUV : R$ 152 mil (promoção de R$ 147 mil)

Geely EX2 : R$ 124.600 Pro / R$ 137.800 Max

MG4 Urban : R$ 135 mil Comfort / R$ 145 mil Luxury / R$ 155 mil Luxury Long Range

Além da concorrência chinesa, marcas tradicionais como Toyota, Jeep e Volkswagen passaram a oferecer promoções para veículos zero-quilômetro.

Mesmo diante desse cenário, a Honda decidiu manter sua política de preços e apostar nos clientes que já conhecem a marca.

A pré-venda foi anunciada para 5 de outubro, com um lote inicial de 3 mil unidades e preços iguais aos da linha 2026. Os valores começam em R$ 117.500, na versão LX, e chegam a R$ 156.400, na RS.

Depois que as 3 mil unidades forem vendidas, a Honda vai aumentar o preço da versão LX em R$ 200. Para as demais configurações, o reajuste previsto é de R$ 1.100.

As vendas regulares da linha 2027 começam no início de novembro. Durante a pré-venda, a Honda também oferece documentação gratuita para quem financiar o veículo pelo banco da própria fabricante.

A montadora informou que não pretende manter os preços promocionais nos lotes seguintes.

A estratégia de preservar as características do City também aparece na política comercial da Honda.

Ao manter os preços de tabela e não oferecer, pelo menos neste início, promoções com descontos muito expressivos, a fabricante contribui para preservar o posicionamento de seus seminovos.

Essa decisão pode ajudar a reduzir os efeitos da desvalorização que atinge veículos usados , especialmente aqueles na faixa de R$ 100 mil a R$ 200 mil. A questão mais complicada para a Honda, porém, vai além do City.

Em momentos de mudanças profundas na tecnologia, no mercado e nos métodos de fabricação, fabricantes tradicionais precisam decidir até que ponto seus produtos devem se transformar para conquistar novos consumidores sem perder aqueles que já são fiéis à marca.

Quando um fabricante enfrenta vendas baixas e tem poucos clientes, uma mudança radical de estratégia pode ser mais simples. Afinal, há relativamente pouco a perder.

A situação é diferente para Honda, Toyota e outras fabricantes tradicionais que construíram uma base de consumidores fiéis. Nesse caso, abandonar características que agradam aos compradores atuais pode representar um risco tão grande quanto deixar de acompanhar as transformações do mercado.

O City 2027 é um exemplo desse dilema . A Honda preferiu atualizar o visual e a tecnologia sem alterar profundamente um produto que já tem um público estabelecido.

Resta acompanhar as vendas em 2027 para descobrir se os consumidores tradicionais aprovaram as novidades e permaneceram fiéis ao City ou se decidiram experimentar modelos concorrentes na mesma faixa de preço.

Honda City 2027 nas carrrocerias sedã e hatch. — Foto: Divulgação / Honda

Preços e equipamentos do Honda City 2027

Os valores abaixo incluem os preços regulares anunciados pela Honda e as condições de pré-venda, quando aplicáveis.

City LX : hatch e sedã R$ 117.700 (pré-venda R$ 117.500)

Assistente de estabilidade e tração (VSA);

Assistente de frenagem de emergência (EBA).

City EX : hatch R$ 137.400 / sedã R$ 138.400 (pré-venda hatch R$ 136.300 / sedã R$ 137.300)

Pacote de assistência à condução Honda Sensing (controle de cruzeiro adaptativo com parada total, frenagem de mitigação de colisão, sistema de permanência de faixa, assistente de evasão de pista e farol alto automático);

Rodas de liga leve de 16 polegadas de alumínio com face diamantada e pintura interna na cor cinza.

City EXL : hatch R$ 144.800 / sedã R$ 145.800 (pré-venda hatch R$ 143.700 / sedã R$ 144.700)

Sistema myHonda Connect (aplicativo de celular para rastreamento, partida remota do motor, acionamento do ar-condicionado à distância e travamento das portas).

City Touring : hatch R$ 153.300 / sedã R$ 154.300 (pré-venda hatch R$ 152.200 / sedã R$ 153.200)

Barra de iluminação em LED que conecta os faróis dianteiros;

Central multimídia com tela de 10 polegadas sensível a múltiplos toques para comandos de volume e mudança de faixa;

Rodas de liga leve de 16 polegadas com pintura interna na cor preta;

Acabamento interno na cor cinza claro (configuração exclusiva para a carroceria sedã com pintura externa nas cores Branco Topázio, Azul Cósmico ou Cinza Basalto).

Teto, capas dos retrovisores, antena e aerofólio superior com pintura preta;

Para-choque traseiro exclusivo com seção central inferior dividida em três partes;

Emblemas da configuração posicionados na grade e na tampa traseira;

Rodas de liga leve de 16 polegadas com pintura preta e aplicação de verniz escurecido;

Revestimento interno do teto na cor preta;

Bancos e demais revestimentos da cabine com costuras vermelhas;

articles.title: iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8: Is $2,000 worth it?
articles.summary: Apple's iPhone Duo reportedly outlasted the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 by over three hours in battery tests, but its weight and repair costs raise concerns.
articles.body: How much would you pay for a phone that turns into a small tablet? Apple is betting the answer is nearly $2,000. After seven years of watching Samsung build folding phones, Apple has finally entered the race with its first-ever foldable iPhone. The new iPhone Duo, which went on sale Oct. 23, opens like a book to reveal a 7.6-inch screen. Its biggest competitor, Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, offers the same screen size and a remarkably similar design. However, Samsung's phone is lighter and costs about $100 less. Apple has some interesting advantages of its own, including impressive battery performance and a clever screen designed to reduce glare. But there are compromises on both sides, including a repair bill that might make you think twice about carrying either phone without protection. So, has Apple finally cracked the folding phone formula, or does Samsung still have the better idea? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. 8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT Apple enters the foldable phone race seven years late Samsung introduced the original Galaxy Fold in 2019. Those early devices came with plenty of growing pains, including concerns about screen durability. Since then, Samsung has steadily improved its folding technology. Apple took its time. In fact, we covered one of the company's early ideas in our article about Apple's foldable iPhone patent in 2023. Now the iPhone Duo is finally here, and Apple has made some interesting design decisions. The phone features a polished titanium frame, Apple's A20 Pro processor and a large inner OLED display. It also introduces a redesigned version of iOS built around the folding experience. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 takes a different approach. It uses Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and Samsung's One UI 9 software, which has evolved through several generations of folding phones. That experience gives Samsung an advantage in some areas. However, Apple has already managed to outperform its rival in early battery testing. iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8 price: Prepare for sticker shock Let's get the painful part out of the way. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage. The 512GB model costs $2,199, while the 1TB version jumps to $2,599. If you really want to splurge, Apple's 2TB model costs an eye-watering $3,199. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899.99 for 256GB. The 512GB version costs $2,099.99, while the 1TB model reaches $2,499.99. That puts Samsung roughly $100 below Apple at comparable storage levels. Of course, Samsung has another advantage. Its Fold 8 has been on sale since August, so retailers and carriers have had time to introduce promotions. However, I'd look closely at those deals before celebrating the savings. Some carrier offers require a qualifying trade-in or a lengthy commitment to monthly bill credits. There's also a larger question. When you're already spending nearly $2,000, will saving $100 really determine which phone you choose? I suspect the answer comes down to what happens when you actually hold them. Apple's folding iPhone has a weight problem One of the first things you'll notice about these phones is how similar they look. Both fold horizontally like a book, with smaller screens on the outside and expansive displays when opened. But there's a noticeable difference in weight. The iPhone Duo weighs 8.96 ounces, compared with 7.09 ounces for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's almost two ounces heavier for Apple's phone. If you've ever carried a heavy smartphone in your pocket all day, you know how noticeable that can become. The difference could be even more apparent when you're holding the phone open for extended periods. Samsung also wins on thickness. Its Fold 8 measures about 0.38 inches thick when closed, while the Duo measures 0.44 inches. Apple counters with a rounded titanium design that may feel more comfortable in your hand. Samsung uses sharper edges and a flatter appearance. There's also something worth thinking about. Both phones have relatively small outer screens. Apple's measures 5.4 inches, while Samsung's comes in at 5.5 inches. Those screens are perfectly usable for everyday tasks. However, they're considerably smaller than the displays on many conventional flagship phones. You could end up spending $2,000 on a device that requires an extra step whenever you want a bigger screen. That's why I'd recommend trying both in person before buying. The phone that feels exciting for five minutes in a store needs to feel comfortable after five hours in your hand. The iPhone Duo display has a clever trick Both folding phones open to reveal 7.6-inch OLED screens with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. Each also offers peak outdoor brightness of 3,000 nits. The real difference comes down to how those displays handle reflections. Apple developed a nano-texture finish for the Duo's inner screen. It creates a matte appearance that helps reduce glare and makes the fold crease harder to see. Anyone who has struggled to read a glossy screen near a sunny window might appreciate this approach. Samsung's screen has a more traditional glossy finish, which can make colors appear richer. Some early iPhone Duo reviews suggest Apple's matte display sacrifices a little contrast and vibrancy to achieve its reduced reflections. Neither approach will appeal to everyone. However, Apple has another interesting feature coming. Apple Pencil support could give the Duo an edge The iPhone Duo now supports the Apple Pencil (USB-C) through iOS 27.2, which Apple released on Oct. 26. That means you can sketch or annotate documents directly on the folding screen. The feature already works in the software's release candidate. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 does not support the S Pen. Samsung removed the feature as it pursued thinner folding designs. There is one catch with Apple's approach. The Duo works only with the USB-C Apple Pencil. Even if you already own an Apple Pencil Pro, you won't be able to use it with this phone. The USB-C version also lacks the pressure sensitivity available on more advanced Apple Pencil models. Still, this could be useful for someone who regularly signs documents or prefers handwritten notes. Samsung still understands multitasking better Here's where those seven years of Samsung experience become apparent. Let's say you're on a video call and someone sends you an important document. You want to review it without interrupting the conversation. Then you need to check your calendar. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 can handle several apps on its larger screen. You can run three apps in split-screen mode, and Samsung also offers pop-up windows for additional flexibility. The Fold 8 supports Samsung DeX, too, giving you a desktop-style experience when connected to compatible external displays. Apple has introduced Split View on the Duo, allowing two apps to run side by side. That's a first for the iPhone, and it should make the larger screen far more useful. However, Apple's approach remains more restrictive than Samsung's. Split View uses a fixed arrangement, and you don't get the same floating-window flexibility. There's another issue that early iPhone Duo owners are discovering. Some iPhone apps aren't ready for the bigger screen Apple redesigned iOS 27 for the Duo, which ships with iOS 27.1. Its own apps have been adapted to use the folding display. However, some third-party apps haven't caught up. Early reviewers found that certain apps display large black bars or awkward layouts when opened on the bigger screen. That could be frustrating when you've paid so much for additional screen space. Fortunately, developers can update their apps to support the Duo's design. Some popular apps have already received updates, and more are expected. For now, though, Samsung has a more established folding software experience. I would also pay attention to which apps you use most. A larger screen loses some of its appeal when your favorite apps still behave as though they're running on a much smaller phone. Apple's battery life delivers a welcome surprise Folding phones have a difficult job. They need enough battery power to run a large display without becoming too bulky. Apple's iPhone Duo uses two internal batteries and an A20 Pro processor designed for efficient performance. Samsung equips its Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a 4,800mAh battery and Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip. Both processors offer plenty of power for demanding apps. However, early independent testing suggests Apple has a surprising advantage when it comes to battery life. In one battery test involving continuous web browsing over 5G, the iPhone Duo reportedly lasted 13 hours and 20 minutes, compared with 10 hours and 6 minutes for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's more than three additional hours for Apple. Another independent test produced encouraging results for the Duo. While streaming video over Wi-Fi with the larger screens at maximum brightness, Apple's foldable reportedly lasted 18 hours and 15 minutes, compared with 16 hours and 30 minutes for Samsung. Although the tests used different methods, both suggest Apple has managed to squeeze impressive battery life out of its first folding phone. Apple officially claims up to 31 hours of video playback using the inner display. However, that figure comes from controlled laboratory testing, so everyday results will vary depending on how you use the phone. Charging is another consideration. Apple says the Duo can reach 50% in about 20 minutes with a compatible wired charger. Samsung supports 45W wired charging and fast wireless charging. For anyone who spends long days traveling or regularly finds their battery running low before dinner, Apple's early results are encouraging. THE IPHONE DUO IS OFFICIALLY HERE — GET IT FOR NO MONEY DOWN AT T-MOBILE A $2,000 folding phone still comes with camera compromises For nearly $2,000, you'd expect a phone with an incredible camera. And while both of these foldables take excellent photos, there's a catch. Apple's iPhone Duo has two 48MP rear cameras, while Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 has two 50MP cameras. Neither has a dedicated telephoto lens, which means you're giving up some of the zoom capabilities found on other premium phones. Think about trying to get a close-up shot of your child playing soccer or capturing something interesting in the distance while on vacation. Apple's Duo offers 2x optical-quality zoom by cropping into its main sensor. Samsung uses a similar approach, with digital zoom for subjects farther away. Both can handle everyday photos, but if you love getting those close-up shots, an iPhone 18 Pro Max or Galaxy S26 Ultra may be a better choice. Here's where Samsung throws another option into the mix. Its Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.99, just $100 more than Apple's Duo at their regular starting prices. For that extra money, you get a 200MP main camera and a dedicated telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom. That's worth considering if you want a folding phone but aren't willing to give up a more versatile camera. And with Samsung already offering discounts on some models, you may not even have to spend more. Apple has some fun camera features Samsung can't match exactly Ever try taking a group photo and realize you're the one missing from it? Apple's Smart Take could help with that. Just prop open the iPhone Duo, get into the picture and let its AI recognize when everyone is posing. The phone automatically snaps the photo, so there's no racing against a timer or asking someone else to take the shot. Then there's Duo Preview, which lets the person you're photographing see themselves on the outside screen. That could save you from hearing, "Wait, let me see that one," after every picture. Apple also came up with Kid Cue, which plays Peanuts animations on the outer display to get children to look toward the camera. If you've ever tried getting a toddler to cooperate for a family photo, you can probably appreciate that one. Samsung has a few tricks of its own. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 can show people a preview on its outer screen, and you can prop it partially open for hands-free photos. That comes in handy when you want to be in the picture instead of always being the one taking it. The most expensive iPhone Duo surprise could come after you buy it Now let's talk about something that deserves far more attention than it usually receives. Repairs. Apple rates the iPhone Duo IP68 for dust and water resistance, while Samsung gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 an IP48 rating. That gives Apple stronger protection against dust under standardized laboratory testing. However, neither rating guarantees that a folding screen or hinge will survive years of rough treatment. These phones also contain more moving parts than conventional smartphones. And if something goes wrong, the repair costs can be substantial. There's another reason to think carefully about durability. As we reported in our article, Apple confirms iPhone Duo screen problems after launch. Some owners experienced cracks along the inner screen near the hinge within hours or days of purchase, sometimes during initial setup. Apple acknowledged an issue affecting a small number of devices and directed affected customers to contact AppleCare for replacements. The company hasn't identified the cause or disclosed how many phones are affected. An AppleCare+ subscription isn't required to request a replacement for this acknowledged issue. Still, it's something I'd consider before spending nearly $2,000 on a first-generation folding iPhone. According to Apple's published repair estimates, replacing the iPhone Duo's damaged inner display costs $999 without AppleCare+. That's roughly half the cost of the entry-level phone. Apple also lists an estimated $1,499 charge for certain other damage repairs. There is some relief for minor screen damage. Apple's replaceable inner display cover layer costs $49 to replace without AppleCare+, provided the damage is limited to that layer. AppleCare+ can significantly reduce eligible repair charges. For example, an inner display repair is listed at $99 under the coverage, subject to the plan's terms. Of course, the coverage itself adds to the cost of ownership. Samsung's folding phones also have specialized displays and hinges that can be expensive to repair. However, repair pricing varies by model, damage and coverage. This is one area where I'd encourage anyone considering either phone to look beyond the advertised purchase price. After all, a $2,000 phone is expensive enough without worrying about what happens if it slips out of your hand and you're suddenly facing a repair bill approaching $1,000. Another iPhone Duo change could surprise travelers Apple has made the iPhone Duo eSIM-only worldwide. That means you won't find a physical SIM card slot. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 supports both eSIM and a physical nano-SIM card, although configurations may vary by market. For most people in the United States, this probably won't be an obstacle. Major carriers support eSIM, and many international providers offer digital plans. However, if you travel frequently and prefer buying physical SIM cards at your destination, Samsung gives you more flexibility. It's worth checking whether your preferred mobile provider supports eSIM before buying the Duo. iPhone Duo or Galaxy Z Fold 8: Which should you buy? If you've been waiting years for a folding iPhone, Apple's Duo is an appealing first attempt. It offers excellent early battery performance, an impressive display and the convenience of staying within Apple's ecosystem. However, I wouldn't overlook Samsung. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is significantly lighter, costs a little less and offers more flexible multitasking. Those advantages could become increasingly important once the excitement of owning a new folding phone wears off. And here's something else to consider. If most of your day involves texting or checking email, you may spend far more time using the smaller outer screen than you expect. The larger display becomes especially useful when you frequently review documents or watch videos while traveling. Before buying either phone, think about how much time you would realistically spend with it unfolded. Also, if you're considering switching between Apple and Samsung, take a look at our guide on how to transfer data to a new iPhone or Android at CyberGuy.com. It can help make the move considerably easier. HERE ARE SOME TIPS ON HOW TO ORGANIZE PHOTOS WITH KEYWORDS ON YOUR PHONE Kurt's key takeaways I have to give Samsung credit. Seven years ago, folding phones seemed like an expensive experiment, and I wasn't convinced they'd ever catch on. But Samsung stuck with the idea, and now Apple has finally joined the party. I like what Apple's done with the iPhone Duo, especially the display and those impressive early battery results. Still, I keep coming back to the price. Nearly $2,000 for a phone that's heavier than Samsung's and doesn't have a dedicated telephoto camera? That's a tough sell. And the possibility of a $999 inner screen repair would certainly make me nervous. I also wouldn't count Samsung out just because Apple has entered the race. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is noticeably lighter, and Samsung has spent years figuring out how to make that larger screen useful. Being able to run more apps at once is a nice advantage, especially if you're someone who likes getting work done on your phone. And let's face it, a lighter phone is something you'll appreciate long after the excitement of showing everyone how it folds has worn off. If I were spending this kind of money, I'd want to see how Apple's first folding iPhone holds up after a few months of everyday use. I'd also want to hold both phones before deciding. But here's what I keep wondering. How often would I really open that larger screen? If I ended up using the smaller outside display most of the day, I'd have a hard time convincing myself that spending $2,000 was worth it. Would you really spend $2,000 on a folding phone, or do you think Apple and Samsung are charging us more to solve a problem we never had? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Windows 11 is now ‘up to 40 percent faster’ on PCs with 8GB of RAM
articles.summary: A new Windows 11 update is improving memory usage and performance.
articles.body: Microsoft has been doing a lot of work to improve memory usage and increase performance on Windows 11 PCs over the past year. Last month the company revealed Windows 11 is now “more responsive” and runs better on PCs with 8GB of RAM, and now the company is releasing a new update today that includes further memory improvements. “On 8 GB PCs, Windows is now up to 20 percent more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40 percent faster in our lab test,” says Windows chief Pavan Davuluri. One of the key ways Microsoft has achieved better performance on PCs with 8GB of RAM is through compression. [Media: “As a result, Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return,” says Davuluri. This compression helps Windows avoid writing data to a virtual memory paging file on a disk, slowing down apps and performance. Microsoft is also making improvements across Windows, Edge, and Microsoft 365 apps that reduce “committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB.” Memory improvements in Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook alone add up to 360MB of RAM savings. Windows 11 no longer loads widgets on a PC with 8GB of RAM until you open the widgets panel, saving around 200MB of RAM. Inactive tabs in Edge now sleep after 15 minutes, reducing memory consumption further. While Microsoft is shipping an update to Windows 11 with these memory improvements, the company is still working on improving RAM usage in Windows in the coming months. Memory compression will get “smarter and more efficient” over the next few months, and Windows features and apps will share more common parts like widgets and search sharing a single web engine. Microsoft is also working with PC makers and chipmakers to optimize how much memory a PC needs to reserve for its hardware, enabling more for Windows.

articles.title: Moft’s new origami case adds a kickstand and grip to the iPhone Duo
articles.summary: The Dynamic Folio Case also protects the Duo’s outer screen while it’s banging around with other things in your pocket.
articles.body: Originally released in early 2025 as an accessory for the iPad, Moft has redesigned its Dynamic Folio as a case for the iPhone Duo that does more than just protect Apple’s folding phone. You can use it to prop the Duo up at several different angles for hands-free use, or reconfigure the Dynamic Folio’s origami-like screen cover and use it as a finger grip while you’re holding the phone. The new Dynamic Folio Case for iPhone Duo is now available for preorder through Moft’s online store for $89.99 in navy blue or misty cove plus sapphire color options, with shipping expected to start in mid December. That’s a small bump in price over Moft’s $69.99 Dynamic Folio, but while that accessory attaches magnetically to the back of the Duo for easier removal, the new case version is designed to clip securely to the phone while providing additional protection for the back and the front and rear edges of Apple’s foldable. [Image: Both versions of the Dynamic Folio help protect the iPhone Duo’s outer display from scratches while it’s in your bag or pocket, but that cover also folds multiple ways to function as a kickstand that supports the Duo in landscape or portrait orientations. It can even hold the Duo at an angle in “Lounge Mode” so you can more comfortably use the phone hands-free while lying in bed, or it can function as a PopSockets alternative, although it doesn’t look quite as comfortable to hold as those popular grips.

articles.title: Anupamaa Fame Rupali Ganguly moves Bombay High Court over misuse of AI-Generated photos and morphed videos
articles.summary: Actress Rupali Ganguly, who has been dominating the television screens with her popular show, Anupamaa, recently moved to Bombay High Court taking legal
articles.body: Actress Rupali Ganguly, who has been dominating the television screens with her popular show, Anupamaa, recently moved to Bombay High Court taking legal help against the unauthorised use of her photographs, videos across online and offline platforms. The actor claimed that several platforms and websites are using her pictures without permission. She also alleged that some adult websites are hosting AI-generated fake images and morphed videos featuring her.She has stated that her photographs and videos are used by several online and offline platforms without permission. She also claimed that some booking agencies, artist management companies and websites were using her identity without permission.As per Live Law, the actress moved to the court to protect her identity and stop others from using it without her permission.Her lawyer Sana Khan has reportedly requested the High Court to ask the different websites and platforms to remove objectionable photos and videos. She has also asked for protection against the use of her name, pictures and identity without her permission for business or online purposes.Rupali Ganguly is currently one of the most successful actress of Indian television. She started her career as a child actor with her father Anil Ganguly's film Saaheb. She also featured in Hindi films like Angaara, Do Aankhen Barah Haath as the lead actress. After trying her hands at movies, she made her television debut with daily soap Sukanya. She later went on to feature in shows like Sanjivani, Parrvarish, Sarabhai vs Sarabhai. She has also being a part of reality shows like Bigg Boss and Khatron Ke Khiladi. However, it was Anupamaa which changed things for her.In an earlier conversation with Times of India TV, the actress shared how Anupamaa gave her a new lease of life. She also mentioned that while the audience sees her as Anupamaa, Rupali relates to Monisha Sarabhai in personal life, she said, "This show Anupamaa has made me realise I am Monisha in real life. I want to become Anupamaa who is strong, helps other women and raise social issues. After Sanjivani, Sarabhai vs Sarabhai uplifted me and now Anupamaa has given me a second lease of life. Everyone has started knowing me. So many big people from the industry come and tell me they like my work, our show. They tell my brother we like your sister and her show."Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Google’s Gemini-powered Home Speaker is already on sale for 20 percent off
articles.summary: The Google Home Speaker is on sale for $79.99 ($20 off) at multiple retailers, marking the Gemini-powered smart speaker’s lowest price yet.
articles.body: If you’re looking for a good smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker is down to around $79 ($20 off) in all four colors at Best Buy, Walmart, and Target. That’s the best price we’ve seen for the Gemini-powered speaker, which launched in June and represents Google’s first smart speaker in several years. [Product: Google Home Speaker | In her review, my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy noted that Google’s new Home Speaker offers a nice balance of sound quality, size, and design. It’s smaller than the prior-gen Nest Audio, making it easy to place anywhere in your home. However, despite its small size, it produces loud, clear audio with 360-degree sound. Our own David Pierce even found it sounded cleaner, louder, and sharper than Amazon’s similarly priced Echo Dot Max, though Tuohy preferred the latter’s fuller sound and stronger bass. The older Nest Audio still sounds better overall, but Google’s latest speaker takes up less space and costs slightly less. The Google Home Speaker also offers a few useful smart home upgrades. It supports Matter and includes a Thread border router, allowing you to connect and control a wide range of compatible smart home devices. It’s also the first Google smart speaker that can double as an audio output for the Google TV Streamer 4K, letting you play TV audio through one or two speakers instead of your TV’s built-in speakers. Tuohy found it worked well and delivered clear dialogue, though sound quality varied depending on what she was watching. One of its most notable features is support for Gemini, which is also available on older Google speakers and is much better at understanding natural language and complex requests than the old Google Assistant. In her testing, Tuohy found it could handle multiple smart home commands at once and respond to conversational requests, like turning down the air conditioner when she mentioned feeling too hot. It’s also particularly impressive at answering general knowledge questions, though it can be slow and unreliable at times. Keep in mind, too, that some features require a $10-a-month Google Home Premium subscription, including Gemini Live, which lets you have extended conversations with the assistant without repeating the wake word. Read our Google Home Speaker review.

articles.title: Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
articles.summary: Apple’s new watchOS beta includes a first look at Siri Recap and Live Rewind on Apple Watch.
articles.body: Starting today, Siri can tune into the Apple Watch’s mic with Audio Intelligence features that are available in the new watchOS 27.3 developer beta rolling out now. The two new additions are Siri Recap, which uses “ambient listening” to generate summaries of your conversation, and Live Rewind, which generates text transcripts of the last 15 seconds of audio your watch’s mic detected. Apple is also releasing its redesigned Health app for testing today in the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and announced expanded language support in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese. It adds sections like a new Insights tab with summaries for heart, sleep, fitness, and other data that pop up during the day, a For You section with personalized recommendations, and health content like educational videos and articles. Apple: * Live Rewind, which can help users recall what was just said in conversation. A double-press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so the user can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with. Users can ask Siri about the content of the text or save it to the Siri app to revisit later. * Siri Recap, which can create high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment. When it comes to the implications of an ambient, always-listening AI, Apple has released this Audio Intelligence Privacy Overview (pdf) about how it plans to protect users’ privacy when their watch is listening around the clock. It goes into detail about Apple’s claims that users’ raw audio “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.” According to Apple, “If you use iCloud with two-factor authentication and have a device passcode, any Siri Recap summary or Live Rewind text snippet you choose to save syncs across your devices end-to-end encrypted in the Siri app.”

articles.title: You can’t hit a wrong note when playing along with songs on Casio’s new keyboard
articles.summary: The $400 CT-FS1 features Casio’s Feel Sync technology that helps inexperienced musicians hit only the right notes.
articles.body: Casio announced a new addition to its Casiotone line of portable electronic keyboards with a feature that could help aspiring musicians master skills like rhythm and timing without the frustrations or discouragement of hitting the wrong note. The Casiotone CT-FS1 is available now for $399.99 in a monochromatic black or white version where even the 61 touch-responsive keys are all the same color. It can run on AA batteries or a power adapter but at just under 10 pounds in weight it’s definitely not the smallest of portable keyboards. There’s built-in stereo speakers and Bluetooth connectivity if you’re playing for others, as well as a physical headphone jack. [Image: The keyboard is available in a monochromatic midnight black or alpine white color scheme. The keyboard’s most compelling feature is what Casio calls its Feel Sync technology that works alongside a new Feel Sync mobile app available for iOS and Android devices. Through the app you can import a song file which is analyzed by an algorithm before playing through the keyboard. As you play along with the song the keyboard will only produce notes that match the song’s harmony, no matter what keys you press. You’re still responsible for timing and matching the song’s rhythm, but the keyboard takes care of everything else so you can work on developing your creative expression without being self-conscious about it sounding awful. [Product: Casiotone CT-FS1 | The CT-FS1 can be played like a standard keyboard without the Feel Sync assistance, but because it’s long enough to accommodate two musicians, you can also split the keyboard into two zones. One side works like a traditional keyboard for an experienced musician to play, while the other benefits from the real time Feel Sync corrections.

articles.title: iPhone 18 rumors suggest a bigger battery, higher price next year
articles.summary: A leaker says Apple’s base iPhone 18 will get a price hike alongside battery and chip upgrades when it launches early next year.
articles.body: After Apple raised iPhone prices earlier this year, a new rumor claims it plans to launch the base iPhone 18 with a higher price, too. A Weibo post from leaker Digital Chat Station, spotted by 9to5Mac, says the base iPhone 18 is getting a couple of upgrades with the price hike, including a larger battery and a new 2-nanometer A20 chip. However, it reportedly won’t have the smaller Dynamic Island featured on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The base iPhone 18 wasn’t included in Apple’s fall iPhone launch event, but Digital Chat Station claims it will arrive early next year, in line with previous reports. It’s rumored to launch alongside a second-gen iPhone Air and the iPhone 18e, which Digital Chat Station also mentions. The leaker doesn’t specify how much the iPhone 18’s price might increase compared to its predecessor. All of Apple’s old models, including the iPhone 17, got a $100 price hike in September. Google and Samsung have also raised phone prices by the same amount over the past year, driven by shortages of RAM and other components. Earlier this week, Apple reported record-breaking iPhone sales despite the higher prices.

articles.title: Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
articles.summary: Here are a few first impressions of the Siri Recap and Live Rewind Audio Intelligence features that arrived today in the watchOS 27.3 developer beta.
articles.body: It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge. That said, here are some initial impressions. What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review.) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public. The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone. [Image: The onboarding process is quite clear. Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap on only at the office during weekdays from 1PM to 4PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.) Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two. [Image: [Image: [Image: I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had many organic, lengthy spoken conversations yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a sense for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims. My first Siri Recap was for an editorial planning meeting for a story I’m working on. It was decent at identifying different topics discussed, and I was impressed that it stripped out some sensitive information. Any outsider looking at these notes would be terribly confused. Ironically, it meant that this summary wasn’t the most useful for my job. What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Apple’s said publicly that Siri Recap is meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. That rings true based on my first one. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations. In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.
